But tlie lion, member for North Norfolk while lie praised the acts of the late Sir John Macdonald, could not resist criticising them almost in the same breath. He couid not resist having a fling at the Canadian racific Railway and the terms under which it was built. He condemned the scheme of Sir John Macdonald in regard to the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway as extravagant. But he forgot to say that his own friends, when in power in 1S74, put upon the statute-book of this country a proposition to build that road on terms far more extravagant than those which were afterwards secured by the Conservative gc\ -eminent. They offered $10,000 a mile to begin with, the contractors to receive a sum per mile in excess of that amount which sum was to be agreed upon and to be paid in twenty-five years with interest at four per cent. Besides this the contractors were to have 20,000 acres of land per mile. But the hon. member for North Norfolk forgot to mention that. In his estimate of what the Canadian Pacific Railway, as built by the Conservatives had actually cost, he estimated $62,000,000 in cash and railway works completed, and he took the land grant as being worth $5 or $0 per acre some very high figure
Three dollars an acre.

Yes-$60.000 per mile, and added this to the $62,000,000 given to the construction of the road. Why, when this land grant was given it was worth no such sum as that. It is useless, valueless, without railway communication. We bought the whole country for somewhere in the region of a million dollars
A million and a half-three hundred thousand pounds sterling.

Yet, though the land was worth nothing until the road was

built, the hon. gentleman lias estimated it at tile price which it might afterwards have brought. He forgot to say also that the Canadian Pacific Railway are taking from the Canadian government as part of their land grant nearly 2,000,000 acres of land in a country which was arid, upon which hardly a blade of grass would grow, Intending to spend some $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 in irrigating it, and so giving it value and making it useful. In giving a land grant, we were doing exactly what the people in the United States did-giving a part of the land in order to have it all developed. We did it successfully. The Finance Minister did not say a word about it, he did not say one word finding fault with giving the land for the purpose of building that magnificent work of which we are all so proud.
Now, I may be asked, What scheme do you propose? We are told that the people of Canada are ambitious, that we are on the top of the wave of prosperity, that we are anxious to develop every section of the country. In my opinion, the transportation question is the most important one to settle. Cheap means of communication are essential to our development. I may be asked: What scheme do you propose instead of that submitted by the right hon. gentleman. There are a great many propositions, but none of them involve the absurdity of the proposition of building a line from Winnipeg to Quebec and Quebec to Moncton. It is alleged that we need to do justice to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which has been a great benefit to the country, and has expended large sums of money for which its stockholders have received no return. If it is necessary to give that company an opening to the North-west, if it is necessary, as northwestern men say, to correct what they allege are excessive rates, for goodness sake, let us adopt a sensible plan instead of that proposed by the right hon. gentleman. Let it be left to experts to decide upon which is the best plan and most likely to develop our resources. Let us have some engineer to report upon the subject. Let us not go into this enterprise without any figures, without a single survey, without any technical knowledge of the country. Let us, before making this jump, obtain the fullest possible information. If the Grand Trunk people wanted to get into that section of country, their first proposition was the most sensible one, namely, the extension of the Ontario system of railways to Winnipeg and from Winnipeg to Port Simpson. I think the company's proposition had some merits to commend it, but the government loaded them down for no other reason but political reasons. Why did they force the Grand Trunk Railway Company, if they wanted to go in and develop Manitoba and the North-west, to build a railway to Quebec? Wliy did they force them to take over the Quebec bridge? Why did they Hon. Mr. H AGO ART.
force them to build useless lines of railway in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia? Do the company want to do so? Is it in the interest of the people of the North-west ? No, the people of Manitoba want to get the highest possible price for their grain, they want the cheapest possible mode of carriage for their wheat to the point of consumption. They do not want to load down the people of this country with the enormous debt which is proposed by the right hon. gentleman. Wbat is the debt? The distance from L&vis to Moncton, ns stated by the Prime Minister, is 425 miles.
He estimated it at 400 miles, not 425.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: But he added the curvature, and his statement was that from Ohaudiere Junction, giving what he called a liberal estimate, it was 425 miles. Estimating the cost at $35,000 per mile, you get $15,000,000. The distance from Quebec to Winnipeg is 1,400 miles, and estimating the cost at $35,000 a mile, you get a total amount of $49,000,000. Then there was the little calculation in reference to interest that has to be paid on cost of construction. When I made a statement the other day, I had not read the articles of agreement, I thought the government would pay interest on the money during the construction of the road, and that that was an expenditure not to be calculated in the amount of 3 per cent to be chai'ged to the company. I find upon looking at the agreement that the debentures are issued and guaranteed by the government ns the road is constructed, and that the company become liable for the 3 per cent on the expenditure on the eastern section from the time the government pay over the money. That was the statement of the Minister of the Interior to-day when he corrected me in my calculation. Take the calculation of the Finance Minister. Making a moderate estimate of $35.-0C0 per mile for both of these sections, it amounts to an expenditure of $50,000,000. They have to pay interest. Never mind about our glorious surplus of $15,000,000. By making an actuarial calculation and applying that money we have in hand at; the rate of 3 per cent or 34 per cent interest, what will it amount to? The Finance Minister forgot that he lost interest on it from the time of payment to the time that he expended the money. There is 3 per cent upon $49,000,000.
You are wrong. He allowed for that.
I do not know what the hon. gentleman says ?
He included the interest in his calculation ?

The three per cent payable by the company commences seven
8C97

years after the construction or the handing over of the work and after the company commences to operate. Then, for seven years we have to pay interest on the amount ourselves. During the next three years if the company earn the amount they are obliged to pay the interest, but if they do not earn it, the unpaid interest for three years is capitalized at three per cent. Then the lion. Minister of Finance calculates the distance in the mountain section to be about 450 miles which, at $30,000 per mile, would cost $13,500,000. For seven years we pay upon that amount. We pay the full amount of the expenditure for the purpose of constructing the road from Winnipeg to- Quebec, we pay the full amount of the expenditure for the construction of the road from Quebec to Moncton, we hand the road over to the Grand Trunk Railway Company and pay the interest upon the cost of construction for seven years, and if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are not able to pay the interest during the three years succeeding the seven years term, we add that to the capital account and charge them three per cent upon it. How that obligation is going to cost the people of this country $13,000,000 or $15,000,000 is the most extraordinary tiling I ever heard of. Surely we are expending the money in the construction of the road. We pay out the money for the interest upon it for seven years and these sums of money put together will impose an obligation upon us, as I calculate it and as it is calculated by the hon. Minister of Finance, of $70,000,000. Then, for the purpose of gratifying the people of Quebec who do not really want the road, which will be of no public utility to them, and for the purpose of expending $15,000,000 in the province of New Brunswick we are called upon to add to the debt of this country in the next seven or ten years an amount equal to more than $75,000,000. I will venture to say that when the road is completed you will find that the sum of money expended for the purpose of carrying out this contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will not be $75,000,000 because, as I said before, it is impossible that the road can be constructed for that amount. Having the experience and the knowledge that we have at present as to what roads cost in that section of the country and knowing that the expenditure of the Canadian Facific Railway for the construction of the road from North Bay to Fort William was $00,000 per mile, I do not think it is possible to leave that road in the first-class condition which it is proposed to do with ordinary gradients, not gradients of twenty-one feet to the mile, but ordinary gradients of fifty-two feet to the mile, for less than $125,000.000. What could we do with an expenditure of $125,000,000 ? What works for the development of the country could we construct with that money ? We could have a road, as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway
originally proposed built to Fort Simpson. We could have our waterways enlarged to meet modern requirements which call for a depth of twenty feet, we could have the Georgian Bay canal built, we could have communication between the port of Montreal and tlie city of Quebec and the whole navigation of the St. Lawrence put in first-class condition. I will leave it to the people of this country to say which they prefer. If it is the question of transportation that is first in the minds of the people, if that is the all absorbing question, if it is a question as to what will tend to the development of this country more than anything else, seizing the present moment and making, if you like, a lavish expenditure for the purpose of developing the country upon the lines I propose will accomplish more to render the resources of Canada available than anything else. Cheap transportation will divert the trade of any country from one road to another. We have the experience of the United States. A half a cent a bushel will divert the trade from New York to Baltimore, or to Philadelphia, or to Boston. The expenditure for the building of the Georgian Bay canal would be justified by the results, the parties who Built the canal would get a good return for their investment and you would be enabled to transport to Montreal wheat delivered at Fort William or Port Arthur for five cents per bushel which is nearly the present rate. The whole scheme of transportation ought to be thought out. The government of the country ought to appoint their experts for the purpose of doing it. They ought not to jump in with wild cat schemes for the purpose of developing the country as they pretend it is for that purpose, but there ought to be a thorough investigation, first, to ascertain what the results of any such scheme would be. I am confident that if a commission of experts, men who have studied the question, commercial men, engineers, looked into this proposition not a single man from one end of the country to another would be in favour of the scheme as proposed by the right hon. the leader of the government. We are told that boards of trade are petitioning in favour of it, that the Board of Trade of Toronto and the Board of Trade of Halifax have petitioned for it. I have a great deal of respect for the boards of trade but I have more respect for the intelligence of the people of this country either as exemplified by representatives on this side of the House or by the right hon. gentleman and his supporters on the other side of the House. I have a great deal of respect for boards of trade. Is there any feeling in the country in favour of this proposition Was there any agitation in the country in favour of it ? The hon. Minister of the'Interior read letters in favour of it. I could read letters' to the contrary. He quoted partial remarks by newspapers and he quoted my hon. friend from East Grey

(Mr. Spi'oule) as a supporter of transcontinental roads. He quoted my hon. friend from East Grey as saying that it would require fifteen or sixteen transcontinental roads in the prairie section of the country. What the hon. gentleman said was that to meet the requirements of the people of that section of the country and to carry out their grain in a couple of months it would require fifteen or sixteen transcontinental roads. Do they require anything of the kind ? For the purpose of the trade of that country it would be sufficient to erect elevators in the different sections of the country and large elevators at the ports on Lake Superior at which the grain is received to be shipped out for consumption in foreign countries. That is the proper system to adopt. No railway will put upon its road rolling stock sufficient to move the whole crop of the country in two or three months. It would pay no company in the world. If there was proper rolling stock, and if the elevators were sufficient to store the grain, there is sufficient railway accommodation in that section of the. country at present. The commercial requirements of that country when they arise will be satisfied by railroads which are in existence, and by other railroads which will be developed by the people themselves. There is no necessity for the government entering into such a project, it may be necessary to develop new parts of the country to build railways, but there is no part of the Dominion so well served with railways now as Manitoba and the North-west. I venture to say that there is not 1,000,000 bushels available for sale in that section of the country which has not at present been carried by railroads to the point of shipment. The Minister of the Interior said that the Montreal ' Gazette ' had stated that it was in favour of a line from North Bay to the Pacific, with such branches as the company thought it commercially wise to construct, and that the ' Gazette ' stated that no one would have successfully attacked such a proposition. The Minister of the Interior gave that ns the opinion of one of the leading commercial papers of Canada, the Montreal ' Gazette,' in favour of this scheme, but he forgot to read this portion of the 'Gazette's' article :
This wild project should be dropped until there is time to find out what it means in the country financially and when that Is made plain and thought over by prudent men it will be probably dropped altogether. It is to be regretted that the Grand Trunk project has had these political features appended to It.
That is exactly the view of a great many members on this side of the House. The Grand Trunk Railway came to parliament with a plain commercial proposition. They were anxious to enter into the North-west to compete for the carrying of the immense products of that fertile country. They came with a proposition of their own, but for Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
political reasons, and for political reasons alone, they are loaded down with two useless propositions, namely, the road to Quebec and the road to Moncton. I hope yet that the right hon. gentleman will drop the scheme. I appeal to him not to risk the financial position of the country in an expenditure so ridiculous. If the country north of Quebec has the resources lie thinks, let us develop it as we have been developing it in the past, and as Ontario has been developing the Temagami district ; let us develop it locally toy roads through that section of the country. I have proved conclusively that there is no necessity for this road in New Brunswick. It is a useless appendage. It is a destruction of property at present owned by the government of the country. It will entail on us a loss of nearly $00,000,000 out of the $72,000,000 we have invested in the Intercolonial Railway. You are destroying one portion of your property by erecting a new property. You are giving no better line to accommodate the commerce of the country. Your scheme is ridiculous.
The Minister of the Interior talked about other railways having running rights over this line. The ex-Minister of Railways fully showed the absurdity of that. One would think it was a new power that was given to railroads. Why, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council can grant running powers to any railroad In Canada on any other railroad. What was the object of putting it In this charter and agreement, when it is in the law of the land already ? And yet, the Minister of the Interior told us that the agreement would never have been signed if that clause were not in it. As tlie Minister of Finance truly said, this power may he used as a lever for the purpose of making proper freight arrangements; witli other' roads. It enables a company that lias running powers over another road to make satisfactory arrangements for the carrying of their freight or the exchange of traffic.
Have we the power to grant running rights over tlie main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway to another company ?
Yes.
Under the contract ?

You have it in tlie statute, and it is embodied in the new Railway Bill. The Railway Committee of the Privy Council have the power to grant running rights over any road in Canada to any other road on such conditions as they think right and equitable, and the Railway Committee of the Privy Council lias frequently exercised that power. _ Independent of that, some railroads have it in their charters. You will find it in the new Railway Commission Bill.

The new Railway Commission Bill does not interfere in any way with

the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It does not claim to interfere with their freight rates.
There is no doubt about that-on hired rolling stock.
Why could not the whole stoek_.be hired ?
I do not want to interrupt my kon. friend, but if he will refer to section 35 he will see at a glance that it is not possible for the whole of the rolling stock to be hired.
I read that: 'A mortgage which shall be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property.' That is the only equipment that may belong to this company.
If it belongs to the company my hon. friend speaks of, how could the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway give a first charge on it?
Will they be conforming with the conditions of this contract if they lease this equipment and put it on the road?
Not for the $20,000,000 of equipment.
Not to the extent of the $5,000,000?
Not to the extent of $20,000,000.
Then, I would judge from what has been said by the exMinister of Railways and Canals that they can do it to the extent of $15,000,000.

They must be in a position to give on that $20,000,000 of equipment a first charge to the government. They may get the property as they choose, so long as it is once on the road, it is liable to the first charge of the government.
How could it be unless they owned it?
That is the answer.
You are putting a supposititious case.

If I am the owner of equipment or rolling stock and lease it to a company and agree to waive my charge in favour of the government, I have a perfect right to do it. It is a very simple thing.
Mr. GOURLEY'. But the owner would not waive it.

Then we are to understand from the Minister of Justice that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have to put $20,000,000 worth of equipment on that road free from any mortgage, lien or anything else to any other company. If not. I am correct in my statement that they need not put on one cent of rolling stock
except the $5,000,000 worth which will be liable to the government lien.
If my hon. friend be correct, then the contract is badly drawn. That was not the intention of the parties.

The intention of the parties is another thing. The Minister of Justice says that under this clause the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway or transcontinental railway, have to put $20,000,000 worth of stock upon that road, which will go. without any other incumbrance, as security to the government.
That is right.

I am glad to hear that such is the case, because that is a further security for the expenditure of $13,000 per mile and $30,000 per mile. I have no doubt that that was the intention, but I doubt very much whether the agreement covers it. We may take it for granted that the Grand Trunk Railway are obliged to put $20,0000,000 of stock upon the road, which will be security to the government for the loan of $13,000 per mile from the prairie section to Winnipeg and the loan of $30,000 per mile upon the mountain section. Then I see another clause- which provides that $24,000,000 of common stock, shall be taken by the Grand Trunk Railway, for which they may not pay a dollar, and be held by it as security for any advance or any endorsation or any agreement which they enter into. They get that stock for nothing, and it may be necessary to be held by them for the purpose of controlling the stockholders of the transcontinental railway. I hope that the government will take proper means to see that every dollar the company expends is accurately shown, so that the government guarantee will not cover more than 75 per cent. But that is a very difficult undertaking, for we know how railway companies and contractors whip the devil around the post, to use a popular expression. The government have no security at ail that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will carry out its agreement except the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway. The hon. Minister of Finance has said that the old Grand Trunk Railway, with its enormous properties, with its assets to the extent of $250,000,000, is at the back of the concern. Weil, the obligation of the Grand Trunk Railway to the government of this country is to be valued by the measure of the Grand Trunk Railway stock. What does it sell for in the market? Does this bargain have a preference over the stockholders, the debenture-holders, and the bondholders? Not at all. You have no security, therefore, with reference to any part of this agreement. All you have is the promise of the Grand Trunk Railway, whatever the value of that may be. Long

ago we advanced a sum of money for the purpose of constructing the old Grand Trunk Railway, which that company was to return. Our claim was superior to everything else on the road, but we found it necessary to put it behind all the other securities except the common stock. To-day the Grand Trunk Railway owe the people of this country a sum, with interest, in the neighbourhood of $30,000,000. That sum we never intend to collect. It is a virtual gift ito the Grand Trunk Railway. We could not collect it if we wanted to, and might just as well make it a present. If we could not collect this sum, of what value is the promise of the Grand Trunk Railway ? I hope and expect that the Grand Trunk Railway will carry out its agreement. It has an' excellent agreement. It will have a road from Quebec to Winnipeg which will cost it nothing for the first ten years and from Quebec to Moncton, and it will have nearly all the money required for the construction of the prairie and mountain sections. All it will have to raise is sufficient money to build a branch from its main line to Lake Superior, and I suppose it may build a line to North Bay, or it may connect with the Temiscamingue road, which is being built by the Ontario government. That portion of it is a good investment. I think they will have no trouble in raising money on the security of that portion of the road from Winnipeg to Lake Superior. I hope the Grand Trunk will be in a position to carry out that part of their contract. Their original proposition for a connection with their Ontario system and the making of a transcontinental road in that way would, I believe, have been in the interest of the country. But, I must protest, as I said before, against the enormous expenditure into which the government seeks to force us. My hope is that when the engineering parties examine the New Brunswick section and the Quebec section, their reports of the cost of building a commercial road there will be so alarming that the government will be compelled to back out of that portion of the scheme. And, if that should occur, I am sure that none will be more rejoiced than the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It would take two years to locate the line from Winnipeg to Moncton, before a dollar can be spent in construction. Hon. gentlemen speak of having the road built within five years after it is located. If the expenditure is to be in the neighbourhood of $35,000 per mile, and if the work is to be carried on under government supervision in a country where they can only commence the work at the two ends- taking the supplies up the Canadian Pacific and commencing construction near the Montreal river, and, on the other hand commencing construction at Quebec-it will require, under the system of contracts and with the contractors which the government can employ, not less than seven ygars to 273
build that section of the road. So, it will be nine years and possibly more before the road will be in a condition to be handed over as part of the Grand Trunk transcontinental line. Interest must be paid on the money used on construction during that time. The parts that are built must be kept up, and, if possible, used. It is an enormous undertaking ; and, as I have said, I hope the the government, on looking into it, will grow alarmed and that the road will not be built. And when the facts are known to parliament and to the people of this country, I feel sure they will never allow such a gigantic expenditure for so useless a purpose.

Mr. Speaker, I should be loath to interject myself in this discussion after the very able and exhaustive speeches to which we have listened, were it not that I come from a province that has been represented for a long time in the councils of the country by the gentleman who has the leadership of the criticism of the project, now before the House. And I would the more hesitate to take part on account of the fact that that lion, member has been for many years my political leader, not merely in the arena of Dominion politics, but in the more restricted arena of provincial politics in the province of New Brunswick. However, I must deal with this question. I trust I shall deal witli it briefly, and I hope to deal with it on broad national lines. I shall endeavour to deal with it from the standpoint of Canada and not merely from the standpoint of the province from which I come. And, in so dealing with it, I shall not have reference to persons, except in so far as they may have relation to facts stated, principles enunciated and conclusions drawn. We are told that this scheme has been precipitated upon the country, that it has been forced headlong into the arena. I think that before dealing with that, I should, for a moment, refer to the speech of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) on that question of precipitation, I shall be called upon to cite one exMinister of Railways and Canals against another ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. It will be a case of the city of St. John vs. the riding of South Lanark. We have listened to a long, a somewhat long, discussion of this subject by the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart). In arising to address the House that hon. gentleman said he proposed to briefly give his reasons for opposing the Bill. I would not wish to say anything derogatory of that hon. gentleman, but I am sure that his speech showed a poverty of argument, while it was resplendent with affirmation and assertion. [DOT] On the question of precipitation, at the very outset I would invite the attention of hon. members to a speech delievered by the hon. gentleman himself. We are told that there should have been delay, that



there should have been deliberation, and then more deliberation, that the country is not prepared for this scheme, that parliament receives it' unprepared, and that the scheme itself has not been matured as it should have been before being brought before the House. In the speech to which I refer, delivered in this House on the 26th of May last, the hon. member for South Lanark made this statement:
The Grand Trunk Railway has done a great deal towards the development of this country, and the stockholders of that concern have had m but meagre return on the amount they have ' invested. Anything the Canadian people can do in return for the great benefits that that company has yielded to this country ought to be done, other things being equal. If they propose to build a road which will open up a new territory in the North-west and make a connecting line with Quehc, I would rather see it assisted than any other scheme I hear proposed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I rise to a point of order, the hon. gentleman is referring to a previous debate. The Prime Minister applies that rule every time he gets an opportunity to lion, gentlemen on this side of the House, and I ask that you apply it now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is well known to the House that no bon. member can quote from a previous debate. We are all quite conversant with that rule.
Would you allow him nevertheless to go on and make his quotations ?

I think it would save time if I were permitted to read the extracts which I have before me, they are iu print. Perhaps I could state from recollection what the hon. gentleman said, but as he has given me permission, I will read it, because it will recall to his mind what he did say, and said very well at that time.
There is no necessity for a commission as to railways. That commission might have been appointed before this session and the government might have formulated some policy, because now is the time to formulate a policy and to build the works that are necessary. The day of depression may come within a year or t.wo, because this country cannot always be in the position which it is at present, and it should take advantage of the tide. A few years is a great deal in the history of a country, as it is in the history of a manufacturing enterprise We should take advantage of the opportunity at the present time to divert the traffic into this section of the country while the routes are being formed, because once you have traffic going in a certain direction it is almost impossible to turn it into another channel. Take advantage of the present tide in our favour. Canada is in a better position now than she will be for a number of years to come to adopt a definite transportation policy, because'this is a state of affairs that cannot continue for a number of years. Take advantage of the present, formulate some policy which is destined to build up this country, take advantage of the opportunity which nature has afforded us, because we are now in the best possible position to secure for ourselves a place amongst the foremost peoples on the face of the globe.

I might also say that those words uttered by my hon. friend from South Lanark were the very words which were uttered by the right hon. leader of this House, in his speech explaining the scheme now before the House. Another extract which I am sure will he of interest to the House, is this :
My opinion is that if the government should decide to give any assistance for that purpose, the company which is entitled to the preference is the Grand Trunk Railway Company. That company has done a great deal to open up this country, they have spent a great deal of money, and have received very little returns for it. it may be the fault of the mangement of the company, but the fact remains that for the vast sums of money which that company has invested and which have had the effect of developing this country more than any other railway except the Canadian Pacific Railway, it has received very little return in the way of profits. I think the policy of the government should he to have this road built as far north as possible, to pass as r.ear as possible to the height of land in order to tap a region of country which has- not been opened up at present.
These words uttered by my hon. friend were prophetic. Little did he realize then that the government perhaps had under consideration just such a policy as he approved of, just such a policy as he deemed in the interest of the country. To-night we have listened to him discussing, first the section between Quebec and Moncton, and then the section between Quebec and Winnipeg. At that very time the Railway Committee were discussing the very scheme which is involved in this Bill. There was involved the completion of a railway from Quebec to Winnipeg, and my hon. friend, by his then spoken words, approved of that policy, the policy which has since been adopted by this government. It is true the hon. gentleman has taken exception to that portion of the scheme between the city of Quebec and the city of Moncton. He has done so in a very laboured way, I am bound to say, a'nd, lie lias done so, it seems to me, on false-premises. In the first place, he has called to his assistance certain statements made by Sir Sanford Fleming, issued in 1804, and be lias endeavoured to show that these reports confirm him in his objections to the route which is now proposed. Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the route between Moncton and Quebec is a line of railway which extends back from Levis to Edmundston. then down the River St. John, to about tlie centre of the province, and then, down one of the tributaries of the Miramlchi, crossing the Nashwaak river, and thence on to Chip-man and to Moncton. My hon. friend has stated here that according to the report and survey of Sir Sanford Fleming the line thus traversed was one that, to use his own words, would not be one mile shorter, that is, the distance between Levis and Moncton would not be one mile shorter by that route than the distance between Levis, or Quebec, and Moncton by the Intercolonial. Has he taken ns into his confidence, so far as to

explain to tliis House that the surveys to which Sir Sanford Fleming made reference were the surveys made between Riviere du Loup and Edmundston and Moncton ? An entirely different route, a route that lengthens the line by nearly one hundred miles. He has not taken into consideration the fact that ltivifire du Loup is situated 123 miles from the Quebec bridge and he has not taken-into consideration the fact that when you travel down by the present line of the Intercolonial Railway to Riviere du Loup, or formerly the Grand Trunk line between Levis and Riviere du Loup, you travel a distance of 123 miles and that thence you cross over the intervening territory, a distance of 85 miles to Edmundston. He has sought to show by these reports that it was an Impracticable line, that it was one which would be condemned and was condemned by the engineers. I am sure that if he had sought information from Sir Sanford Fleming he would have found out that he did not know in very truth that the short line to which he refers is the line between Rlvi&re du Loup and Edmundston, that when you leave Riviere du Loup and travel out over the Temis-couata railway, because that railway traverses one of these routes, you go out seven or eight miles and reach a point on that railway where you have to climb 1,300 feet over the height of land, that you have to do that in sixteen miles, that on reaching the height of 1,300 feet you have to travel down again within a distance of sixteen miles and then you are on the same level from which you started seven or eight or nine miles out from Riviere du Loup. That is all the explanation that is necessary in reference to the statement that is made as to the impracticability of the route between Rivifire du Loup and Edmundston and down the river.	Now, my hon.
friend has not disclosed to us the fact that there was, later on, in the year, I think, 1890-1 am not sure as to the date- an application before the government of Canada, then led by the late Rt. Hon. Sir John Macdonald, for assistance for a railway from Montreal down through the centre of the province of New Brunswick to Moncton and that there was a survey made. Some twenty-five years after the survey made by Sir Sanfcrd Fleming, there was a survey made from Edmundston to the city of Moncton and that survey was made by the Temiscouata railway company in" conjunction with or under the direction of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and that survey located a splendid line. I have had information from eminent engineers, two of them whom I could name, that the line that was then located is one of the best lines, and would prove to be one of the best lines that there is in the province of New Brunswick, and that it will prove to be one of the best lines there is in Canada. I have received within the 273i
last two or three days a letter from an engineer who was engaged in that survey confirming the statement I have made and this route does not follow down the valley of the river St. John as stated by my hon. friend. He has quoted from the report referred to showing that any line between Edmundston and Moncton must necessarily follow down the valley of St. John, and he took us down the present location of the Canadian Pacific Railway to AVcodstock, then he took us either by the back country or by the river route following the curves of the river down to Fredericton. He could reach Gibson by either route. No doubt these routes are excellent ones. I do not call them in question, but, I do know these are not central routes. Neither is a central route through the province of New Brunswick, neither is the shortest route, and neither of these routes which are condemned by Sir Sanford Fleming is the route to which I make reference, the one that was surveyed in 1890, the one that is capable of being on a line for through traffic and on a line for opening up a vast extent of rich country. I shall not refer particularly further to the route between Quebec and Moncton. I shall reserve that for observation a little later on in connection with some other remarks, but, I am only referring to it to show how illusory were the remarks of the hon. member for South Lanark in respect to his condemnation of the present scheme- . the scheme to build a line of railway back of the Laurentian hills, or what you will call the Laurentain recks back from Levis, through that rich section of country, through the counties of Bellecbasse, Mont-magny, and other counties upon the borders of the province of New Brunswick, skirting around that projection of the state of Maine which comes up too far, alas for the good of Canada into our territory, going down to Connors' station and following down the river St. John to Edmundston, going from thence down to Grand Falls and on through a section of country splendid for the building of a railway, because I speak whereof I know, having travelled over ever foot of it myself. I have driven oyer the road in my official capacity as Chief Commissioner of Public Works in New Brunswick. I know the topography of the country, and I know whereof I speak. More than that, it is a land rich in its agricultural resources. Along that line are to be found some of the richest sections of country that are to be found in the whole province of New Brunswick. Then, in that section there are to be found rich timber lands which will be tapped by this railway. I think that the hon. member for the city of St. John in referring to this section of the country did justice neither to himself nor to the province which has for so many years honoured him when be said that that section of the country was not worthy of consideration, or he said that in effect because he said that when you skirted the

northern section by the Intercolonial Railway and skirted the southern section by the Canadian Pacific Railway, you traversed the only sections of the province that were worthy of receiving consideration in the way of building railways. There is that great central part of the province of New Brunswick that is practically untouched by the hand of man. There is that great section of country from the Nashwaak bridge on towards Moncton. I have had occasion to travel through what is known as the Gaspereau valley and I venture the assertion that it is one of the richest valleys, one of the most promising agricultural sections, one of the most beautiful spots that I have ever visited in the province of New Brunswick, and I am sure that the Annapolis valley does not present a prettier picture than the valley of the Gaspereau situated in the heart of one of the finest agricultural sections of the country. It was at one time in the history of the province occupied by people, but the people did not expect that railways would be built and many of them deserted that section because the"y had no railway facilities. I am sure that it certainly cannot be said of that section, near as it is to rich coal fields, that it is unworthy of the consideration of the parliament of Canada, that it is unworthy of being considered in the way of development by the construction of railways. But, perhaps I have digressed from the course of my remarks in speaking of this. I have spoken of it because of the knowledge that I have of it and I have spoken of the feasibility of that route by reason of the fact that I have information from men who are eminent in the engineering profession, from men who know whereof they speak, and I think that their report is worthy of consideration.
Tlie hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has said that the line via Edmundston and Woodstock will not shorten the distance to Moncton by one mile as compared with the Intercolonial Railway. The hon. gentleman should apologize' to the House for having misled it. He should apologize for attempting to make out that the route surveyed from Rivi&re du Loup is identical with the route to be followed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Another feature of the speech of the hon. gentleman (Hon Mr. Haggart) was that it echoed the cry that the Intercolonial Railway was to be denuded of freight, and he asked the House : How about the competition with the Intercolonial Railway in the carriage of freight from St. John when this new road is constructed ? Well, let me in turn ask the hon. gentleman : How about the competition between the Intercolonial Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway from St. John to Quebec and to Montreal ? He alleged that the Intercolonial Railway would be injured because the new line will shorten the distance between St. John and Montreal and Quebec, as compared with the Intercolonial

Railway. It is true that the distance will be shortened. Rut did not the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway short line through the state of Maine shorten the distance between St. John and Quebec and Montreal, and has not the Intercolonial Railway ever since been obliged to compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway for freight and jrassengers. Did the Conservative government in the eighties think of the competition that would be afforded to the Intercolonial Railway when they subsidized the Canadian Pacific Railway short line, even though that short line traversed the state of Maine. I wonder what the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) thought about that. Well, at this date, there need be no alarm, because if the Intercolonial Railway during those years has successfully competed against the Canadian Pacific Railway, it surely can compete against the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) described the line from the Chaudi&re to Moncton as a mad scheme and as an impracticable scheme, and ns a squandering of the money of Canada. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman was a member of the Conservative government in 1890, but whether or not it must be within his knowledge that negotiations were (pending and promises made by the government of Canada, represented by its then distinguished leader, Sir John A. Macdonald, that there should be constructed a line from Edmundston to Moncton through the centre of the province of New Brunswick by way of Chip-man, practically over the route which is now contemplated. Was that a mad scheme? Was that scheme unworthy of consideration? It received the promised support of the government, but it met its fate like the Harvey and Salisbury line, whether in the Senate or not I am not aware, but it certainly did not materialize.
No; it was refused by the government; I remember it well.
But it was promised by Sir Hector Langevin on the floor of parliament.
It was objected to by Sir John Macdonald for the simple reason that it was a competitor with the Intercolonial Railway.
Witli the Canadian Pacific Railway, you mean.
There was no subsidy given to it.

Well, it might have been a competitor with the Canadian Pacific Railway, but isn't it a wonderful thing that the Canadian Pacific Railway was not refused entrance into New Brunswick because it would be a competitor of the Intercolonial Railway. My hon. friend, in a

fine frenzy, almost agonizingly asked : Wliat was tlie use of building this railway through the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The hon. gentleman must have forgotten that this line will not reach within hailing distance of Nova Scotia. There is a tradition in the provinces by the sea that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) was Minister of Railways and Canals for a number of railways, and that he once travelled over the Intercolonial Railway. It is said that he travelled through on a private car with locked doors, which was thought to be a reflection upon the people whom he might meet, although these must necessarily have been his own political friends. It is also rumoured that in the city of Moncton, where the general offices and the great workshops of the railway are situated, the hon. gentleman actually remained for one half hour. If that be true, and that was the only time the hon. gentleman went over the Intercolonial Railway, he may be pardoned for stating to-night that this new railway is to be forced through the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman has spoken of the debt to be incurred by reason of the construction of this line between Moncton and Winnipeg. But he has apparently not listened with any spirit of receptivity to the statements which have been made with regard to that matter. The hon. gentleman must know that it was clearly shown by the Prime Minister when he presented this measure to the House, and as clearly shown by the Finance Minister later, that the obligations on the country involved in this scheme will not exceed $14,000,000. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) does not discriminate between the guarantee of the bonds and the expenditure of money. It is true that there is to be an expenditure of money in connection with the building of the line between the city of Moncton and the city of Winnipeg; but it is also true that after a certain period the interest on that expenditure is to be paid by the Grand Trunk Pacific; and it is also true that the guarantee of bonds on the prairie and mountain sections is simply an endorsement by the government, and not an obligation which will fall upon them. It is simply tantamount to the government of Canada taking collateral security and becoming responsible for an amount which they will never be called upon to pay.
After expressing the opinion that the indebtedness of the government would be very great, the hon. gentleman calls upon the government to halt. He wants time for the whole scheme to be thought out, and he asks the government not to jump into it with precipitation. He thinks there should be a transportation commission; and yet his utterance of to-night was contradicted by his utterance on the floor of this House on
the 26th of May last, to which I have already referred.	.
I do not think there is anything further in the utterances of my hon. friend upon which I need dwell, and I will turn my attention to the remarks which I have to make apart from the hon. gentleman's participation in the discussion.
We ought to realize that there is involved in the proposal before this House a really revolutionary action on the part of governments with respect to aid to railways. We are all familiar with the past history of railway subsidies. We are all familiar with the fact that heretofore the Dominion parliament has granted subsidies to assist in the construction of railways throughout this Dominion, which were supplemented in some of the provinces at least, by provincial aid. I know that has been true with respect to the province from which I come- that year after year the government of Canada aided the construction of railways in that province, and the province almost impoverished itself in endeavouring to aid these railways. I will not refer to the history of the Dominion in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway. That has been referred to many times, and is fresh in the minds of all. But I think I can take you into my confidence in respect to what has transpired in the province of New Brunswick, where many lines were aided by this parliament. I do not think what is known as the New Brunswick Railway was aided by the parliament of Canada. It may have been. That is the line of railway running from Edmundston down to Woodstock, thence to Fredericton, and also from Woodstock out to McAdam junction. But this particular line from Edmundston to New-burg junction, and thence to Gibson, opposite the city of Fredericton, received from the province of New Brunswick aid to the extent of 10,000 acres of land per mile. The best lands in the province of New Brunswick to-day are owned by the New Brunswick Railway and Land Company or its successors. Reference was made to the fact that the proposed railway from Quebec to Moncton traverses this extensive area of land formerly owned by the province and given as a subsidy, and these lands are now the subject of negotiation between the company which owns them and the government of the province. I believe there is an option oil these lands- why ? Because they are splendid settlement lands, and because they are richly timbered, and the line of railway proposed in this scheme will traverse that extensive area of rich agricultural and timber lands. The lines of railway which were aided by this parliament and by the province were as follows : There was the Albert Southern, a line some twenty miles in length, in tlie county of Albert ; there was the Harvey branch ; and there was the St. Martin's and TJpham line. These three lines, though aid-

ed by the government of Canada, and though contributed to by the people of the province, are to-day closed, and are nothing but streaks of rust; there is no evidence of their running. There were other lines-the Elgin and Havelock, which is running ; the Albert Railway, the Kent Northern and the Short Line, which runs from the city of St. John on the west side, down through the county of Charlotte to St. Stephen, paralleling, by the way, to use the term as it is now understood by our lion, friends opposite, another line of railway running from the city of St. John to the to-wn of St. Stephen. These two lines join the same cities, just in the same way as the Intercolonial and the proposed line will join Moncton and Quebec. The lines to which I have made reference have all been foreclosed and sold out under the order of the Equity Court. There are other lines in the province-the Caraquet, the Central and the Moncton and Buctouche-which are now practically held by the bondholders. I want to ask, with respect to these lines which are absolutely closed and are of no value to the country or the province, where are the subsidies, and what has been the net result ?' These are but illustrations of the conse-. quences which have followed upon the system which was adopted by the Dominion and the province of subsidizing railways, and I am very glad indeed that these illustrations teach us a lesson. They teach ns, so far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned, that it was fatal to subsidize railways by giving them grants of public lands. While the lands were given to the railways at the nominal value of a dollar an acre, equal to $10,000 per mile, they are to-day held at a valuation, I understand, of $7, and even $10 in some sections, per acre. That certainly proves that the province of New Brunswick would have been wiser had it borrowed the money at that time and held on to its land. With respect to these others, they squandered our subsidies and have not a dollar to show for them, which only shows in contrast the benefits of the scheme adopted by this government.
I do not propose to go over the ground traversed by hon. gentlemen who preceded me, but I want to say this. For a long time there has been throughout Canada a demand for another transcontinental line from ocean to ocean on Canadian territory. Such a road has been advocated in the newspapers arid on the public platform. In the province of New Brunswick its construction has been frequently urged. Throughout Canada the feeling has taken root that we should have a transcontinental line right through Canadian territory from a Canadian seaport on the east to a Canadian seaport on the Pacific. To paraphrase a line in one of the psalms, the idea was that Canada shall have. the ' dominion from ocean to ocean, from the river to the end of the land.' The time has come when we can realize the aspirations

of our people. If in 1871 we could undertake to build a transcontinental line of railway, we would be justified to-day in undertaking to build two or three such lines. There is prosperity on every hand, there is a feeling of hopefulness everywhere, and if we want to keep pace with the aims and aspirations of the people of every province, we will have to push forward this railway scheme. It would be criminal not to do so. The hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) sounded the alarm when he said that unless we did something now, traffic would seek other channels, and we all know that once traffic has found a certain channel, it is almost impossible to divert it into others. It has been very truly said that the world was born again with the introduction of railways, and I am sure that the Dominion of Canada would almost experience a new birth, if this line were completed and we were in a position to put it into operation. There would then be such a tide of immigration, such a volume of traffic, that another line of railway would be a paying investment. There are so many changes in industrial, commercial, social and political relations, following the establishment of railways, that one can hardly tell, from one year to the other, what the conditions may be twelve months hence, and we have to adjust ourselves to the new and varied conditions. The extension of a railway into new and remote territory increases the value of our lands and other resources. New sources of supply are tapped, traffic increases, and with the increase of traffic there is not only a rise in value of the property along either side of the railway but an increase in the value of other property as well.
One thing which cannot fail to strike anyone who gives any study to this scheme is that it will be the greatest immigration agency Canada ever had. When you realize that the old Grand Trunk Railway, with its tens of thousands of shareholders in the old land will become an active immigration agency, when you realize that each of these 40.000* (I am told that is the number) shareholders will be an immigration agent for this country, you will have some idea of what benefit this policy will be to the Dominion. Every one interested in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway and their securities will advertise Canada's resources; and both the Grand Trunk Railway and this company will be the greatest colonizers Canada has ever had- far more so than the Canadian Pacific has ever been. In this respect this scheme will be worth all the money Canada will have to expend upon it. There is another feature. We must all realize that the extension of a railway into new and remote districts increases the value of our public lands. Take the Canadian Pacific Railway as an example. The value of the lands bordering that railway justify alone the expenditure incurred in the construction of that road.

speechtext: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. .Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved the adjournment of the House.

maintopic: ADJOURNMExNT-GERMANS IN CANADA, AND NAVAL SERVICE.
speechtext:
Before the House adjourns, I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Militia (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) to an item in the Montreal ' Gazette,' concerning the arrival of a German war vessel in the harbour of Montreal and the recruiting of officers and sailors for the German navy. The item reads as follows
On the occasion of the visit of the ' Gazelle,'
however, an exception is being made-
-with regard to recruiting arrangements-
-and the young Germans residents in Canada are to be afforded an opportunity of entering upon service with the 'Gazelle ' without the necessity of going to one of the German ports. The announcement has been made by the imperial German consul that a medical examination of young Germans as to their fitness for military service will be held by the surgeon of the warship on Saturday, at 2 p.m., at the German consulate, 100 Sherbrooke street. No previous notice is necessary ; the young men should bring along their papers. He also states that Germans who wish to do their military service with the German navy may enter upon service right here with the ' Gazelle.'
What I wish to ask is if it is customary or right to allow recruiting by a foreign country in Canada, and, if not, whether tlie minister's attention has been drawn to this item ?

maintopic: ADJOURNMExNT-GERMANS IN CANADA, AND NAVAL SERVICE.
speechtext: I cannot warrant my information on this subject, but I think I am not far astray in what I am about to say. There is no recruiting by the ' Gazelle ' of any officers or sailors for the German navy. So far as that point goes, I am pretty sure I am correct in saying that this refers to young Germans in Canada who are still German subjects and are here only temporarily. According to the laws of Germany these young men, German subjects, are liable to conscription and to serve when called upon in the military or naval service of their country. As I understand it, these young men are taking advantage of the presence of German man-of-war in the port of Montreal to pass an examination which otherwise they would have to go to their own country to pass, because, if they did not pass this examination they would be liable to some penalty. That is the information I have received to-day. I have bad no opportunity of conferring with my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence, but I observed the statement in the press, and we have been making inquiries to ascertain whether my information on the subject is correct or not. We shall have full information in a short time.
speakername: Tlie PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.05 p.m.
Friday, August 14, 1903.
